newsitem.title: USA: Judge awards mother custody in Culkin case. [CORRECTED 02:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Judge awards mother custody in Culkin case. [CORRECTED 02:30 GMT]

text.p: A judge Thursday formally awarded the mother of child actor Macaulay Culkin sole custody of him and his siblings and control of the "Home Alone" star's $17 million fortune.

The children's father, Christopher "Kit" Culkin, withdrew from the custody case on Tuesday and offered to give sole custody to the mother, Patricia Brentrup, after a long dispute. The couple, who have seven children, never married.
In a five-page decision, Manhattan Supreme Court Justice David Saxe said Brentrup is a "fit parent" and "it is in the children's best interests to award sole custody of the children to her."
The careers of the children who are Hollywood actors -- Macaulay (corrects from "Mcauley"), 16, and Kieran, 14 -- will be managed by their mother, the judge decided.

"... Macaulay and Kiernan insist that they will not work with Mr. Culkin," the judge wrote. Saxe issued his decision after hearing closed-door testimony for nearly two hours from Macaulay and his brother, Rory, 7.
Brentrup filed for custody of the children in 1995 and has accused their father of trying to destroy their acting careers. She had also accused Culkin, 51, of excessive drinking and physical abuse.
He has accused her of allowing the children to run wild.

Macaulay (corrects from "Macauley") Culkin, who rose to stardom in "Home Alone," has let it be known that he prefers living with his mother. He also appeared in "Home Alone 2" and "Richie Rich" and has earned about $17 million.
"We're finished, we won't be coming back," an elated Stanford Lotwin, Brentrup's attorney, said as he left court.
Brentrup must notify the father of any decisions regarding the children's theatrical careers, however, the judge said.
The judge called the elder Culkin "a demanding, difficult and pugnacious man," but he credited Culkin for having much to do with Macaulay's success.
The judge criticised Brentrup for not fostering "discipline and good study habits."
"Put bluntly, the older children have done poorly in school, and some of them appear to have learning problems," Saxe said."
The other children involved are Quinn, 12, and Christian, 10. Twenty-year-old Shane and 18-year-old Dakota are not involved in the custody case.

The judge awarded the father "reasonable visitation" with his younger children. "It is hoped that with the passage of time and some family therapy, Mr. Culkin's relationships with his older children will heal and visits with them will resume as well," he said.
